defaults.permitted_development: Across Tyne and Wear, most dropped-kerb schemes are decided first through the highway authority because the crossing sits within the public highway. That does not guarantee the planning position: access onto a classified road, flats, listed buildings or wider frontage alterations can still mean a planning application is needed.

rules.height_rules: Across Tyne and Wear, a dropped kerb does not have its own building-height rule. What matters is whether the level changes, gradients and any reduction in walls or hedges still produce a safe and workable access.
rules.depth_rules: Across Tyne and Wear, the real depth question is practical rather than formula-based: can a vehicle enter and sit inside the site without blocking the footway? Tight front gardens often fail on that point even before wider design issues are considered.
rules.boundary_rules: Across Tyne and Wear, a dropped kerb is not just an opening in your wall: it affects the public highway, so street furniture, utilities, trees, drainage and visibility can all shape the answer. Boundary alterations often need to be planned alongside the crossing rather than afterwards.
rules.roof_rules: Across Tyne and Wear, roof form is not part of a dropped-kerb assessment, but do not ignore linked structures. If the scheme also adds a canopy, car-port edge, gateway feature or retaining work, those pieces are not automatically covered by the crossing approval.
rules.materials_rules: Across Tyne and Wear, for a dropped kerb, the public-highway build-up is normally specified by the council rather than by the homeowner. On the private side of the boundary, choose surfacing that drains well and will not break up or rut under regular vehicle use.

restrictions.conservation_area: A dropped kerb in a conservation area often needs fuller scrutiny if the proposal affects established front boundaries, historic paving or the character of the street.
restrictions.listed_building: Listed building consent may be required where dropped-kerb works alter the setting or fabric of a listed building, including curtilage walls and entrance features.
restrictions.article4_notes: Article 4 directions or planning conditions can remove the simpler householder route for access and boundary works, so the planning status should be checked before relying only on highway approval.

rules.permitted_development: In Newcastle upon Tyne, a dropped kerb is usually dealt with first as a highway approval issue rather than a standard householder planning application. You normally need the council's vehicle-crossing or dropped-kerb consent to cross the public footway or verge, and planning permission can still be needed for access onto a classified road, at flats, or where wider frontage works fall outside ordinary householder rights.

rules.height_rules: Height is not the main planning test for a dropped kerb, but changes in levels still matter. A scheme can become problematic if raised ground, steep gradients or tall boundary features interfere with safe access.
rules.depth_rules: There is no national planning depth limit, but the access should lead to enough in-curtilage standing space for a vehicle to clear the footway rather than overhang it. Schemes become harder where a car would project onto the pavement or rely on awkward reversing.
rules.boundary_rules: A dropped kerb is not just an opening in your wall: it affects the public highway, so street furniture, utilities, trees, drainage and visibility can all shape the answer. Boundary alterations often need to be planned alongside the crossing rather than afterwards.
rules.roof_rules: A dropped kerb has no roof-related permitted development test. The nearest equivalent design issue is whether any linked canopy, gate feature or retaining structure is being added as part of the access works, because those elements are assessed under their own rules.
rules.materials_rules: Materials matter differently here than on a normal householder project. The authority will usually control the kerb and footway construction, while the private driveway behind it should be robust, well-drained and suitable for repeated vehicle loading.

restrictions.conservation_area: Conservation area status usually makes a new access more sensitive where it removes historic boundary features or changes a traditional frontage.
restrictions.listed_building: Listed building consent may be required where dropped-kerb works alter the setting or fabric of a listed building, including curtilage walls and entrance features.
restrictions.article4_notes: Where Article 4 controls or planning conditions apply, the ordinary householder fallback for access-related works may be removed, so both planning and highways should be checked together.

rules.permitted_development: In North Tyneside, creating a new vehicular access usually starts with highway consent rather than a normal householder application. Lowering the kerb and strengthening the footway are public-highway works, and planning permission may still be required if the site fronts a classified road, the property is split into flats, or the proposal depends on larger engineering or boundary changes.

rules.boundary_rules: Boundary and highway issues usually decide a dropped-kerb application more than any householder rulebook. The authority may object because of sightlines, nearby junctions, parking controls, street furniture or conflicts with utility apparatus.
rules.roof_rules: A dropped kerb does not have a roof allowance. The nearest design equivalent is whether the access proposal includes other built elements, such as retaining walls or covered entrance features, which follow separate planning rules.

restrictions.listed_building: Works to form an access for a listed building often need a heritage check as well as highways approval, especially where original frontage features are affected.

rules.depth_rules: There is no set depth allowance, but the council will expect enough space behind the crossing for safe parking and manoeuvring. An access that leaves vehicles projecting onto the public footway is usually difficult to justify.

restrictions.conservation_area: Within a conservation area, access works that disturb original walls, railings, kerb lines or planting often receive a more detailed planning and heritage check.
restrictions.listed_building: A new crossing serving a listed building can need listed building consent where boundary walls, gates, steps, railings or other historic fabric are altered.
restrictions.article4_notes: A local Article 4 direction or an old planning condition can remove normal householder rights for frontage and access changes, even where the dropped kerb itself still needs separate highway consent.

rules.permitted_development: In Sunderland, most dropped-kerb schemes are decided first through the highway authority because the crossing sits within the public highway. That does not guarantee the planning position: access onto a classified road, flats, listed buildings or wider frontage alterations can still mean a planning application is needed.

rules.height_rules: There is no normal householder height allowance for a dropped kerb. The practical checks are kerb and driveway levels, gradients, and whether boundary walls, fences or banks have to be reduced to keep safe sightlines.
rules.depth_rules: The real depth question is practical rather than formula-based: can a vehicle enter and sit inside the site without blocking the footway? Tight front gardens often fail on that point even before wider design issues are considered.

rules.materials_rules: The main material choice for a dropped kerb lies behind the crossing, because the authority typically dictates the kerb and footway build specification. Durable, well-drained driveway materials are usually safer than finishes that shed water or fail under turning wheels.

restrictions.conservation_area: In conservation areas, forming a new vehicular opening can need a closer planning and heritage review where traditional walls, railings, stone kerbs, paving or trees would be altered.
restrictions.listed_building: If the access serves a listed building or involves curtilage walls, gates, piers or historic paving, listed building consent may be needed as well as any highway or planning approval.
restrictions.article4_notes: Do not assume the highway licence is the only approval needed: Article 4 directions and site-specific conditions can still require a planning application for linked frontage or access works.
